column1: # boru Language Specification: error-taxonomy edge cases
# Edge-case battery over the error system (design/legacy/ERRORS.8.ignore): the
# three raise forms and their payloads, do-boundary reification and
# code routing, taxonomy precision for the native codes, the
# pattern-match no-op contract of `error`, and the boru:test assertion
# words. Companion to error.tsv (the §1-§4 basics live there; nothing
# here duplicates a row from that file). Where a row's natural result
# would be an Any-bounded carrier (a field read off a caught Error),
# it is pinned through a concluding `eq` so the residual stays narrow.
# §1  raise forms — codes, payloads, and rejections

column3: any bare word names the code, not just documented ones
an explicit /q atom names the code like a bare word

column1: do [raise io_error/q "disk"] error [dot code] eq io_error/q
column3: …and the caught code is the same atom
the map form accepts a String code

column1: do [raise {code: "strcode", message: "m"}] error [dot code] eq strcode/q
column3: …which reifies as a code ATOM on the Error value
extra spec-map keys never disturb the code

column1: def e (do [raise {code: nope/q, message: "m", got: [1 2], ctx: {k: 5}}]) e dot got size
column3: a List payload rides the Error intact

column1: def e (do [raise {code: nope/q, message: "m", got: [1 2], ctx: {k: 5}}]) e.ctx.k eq 5
column3: …and a nested Map payload reads through dot chains
an empty spec map has neither code nor message
message is required in the map form
a numeric code is rejected — atom or string only
a bound message binding reads through the String slot

column1: def c io_error/q def msg "disk" raise c msg
column3: GOTCHA: the code slot is /q — a bound word raises code `c`, NOT its atom value

column1: def f fn [[x:Integer] [Integer] [raise too_big "big"]] do [f 1] error [dot code] eq too_big/q
column3: a raise inside a fn body propagates to the caller's do boundary

column1: do [[1 2 3] each [drop raise aa "boom"]] error [dot code] eq aa/q
column3: a raise inside an each body aborts the iteration to the boundary
a deferred list auto-evaluates at the drain — its raise still aborts

column1: # §2a  do WITHOUT error already reifies: the Error is a first-class value

column3: do alone reifies a raised error as an Error value
…of type Error
an Error value sits in a list like any value

column1: def e (do [raise aa "x"]) [e] 0 get is Error
column3: …and comes back out as an Error

column1: def e (do [raise aa "x"]) {err: e} dot err dot message eq "x"
column3: an Error value stored in a map reads back through dot chains

column1: def e (do [raise aa "x"]) e dot code typeof
column3: the code field is an Atom
the message field is an ordinary String

column1: do [raise aa "A"] error [dot code case [aa/q 1 bb/q 2 3]]
column3: route on the first code

column1: do [raise bb "B"] error [dot code case [aa/q 1 bb/q 2 3]]
column3: …the second code takes its own arm

column1: do [raise cc "C"] error [dot code case [aa/q 1 bb/q 2 3]]
column3: …an unknown code falls to the default arm
a successful body never reaches the routing chain

column1: do [raise aa "A"] error [dot code] eq aa/q
column3: code comparison is the frontier-free routing primitive

column1: do [raise bb "B"] error [dot code] eq aa/q
column3: …and distinguishes codes exactly

column1: do [do [raise aa "x"] error [dot message]] error [drop "outer"] eq "x"
column3: the INNER boundary catches; the outer handler never runs

column1: do [do [raise aa "x"] error [dot code]] error [drop 0] eq aa/q
column3: an inner-handled error leaves a plain value the outer error ignores

column1: do [do [raise aa "x"] error [raise "outer"]] error [dot code] eq user_error/q
column3: a handler may rethrow — the OUTER boundary sees the new error

column1: do [do [raise inner_c "i"]] error [dot code] eq inner_c/q
column3: do-without-error reifies; the Error value passes UP as a value, and the outer handler fires on it

do [raise aa "x"] error [var [[e] e.code]] eq aa/q

a multi-value success residual passes through untouched

column1: # §3  taxonomy precision — the native codes fire exactly

column3: MaxInt + 1
below MinInt by subtraction
multiplication past MaxInt
2^62 + 2^62 is exactly 2^63 — one past MaxInt
negating MinInt overflows (|MinInt| > MaxInt)
…but landing EXACTLY on MaxInt is fine
Float overflow is IEEE: it goes to inf, never integer_overflow
an overflowing float LITERAL is rejected at parse — you cannot spell inf by overflow
modulo by a static zero is loud
…and a zero through a binding divides just as loudly
Float division by zero is IEEE inf, not an error
…signed
None does not order against numbers
atoms do not order against strings
booleans do not order against numbers
no overload of a typed fn covers a Boolean argument
…nor a String one — dispatch failures are loud
a bare unknown word is undefined
a dotted chain on an unbound lowercase name blames the root

column1: # §3e  sealed class fields and return-type enforcement
def C class {v:Integer} def c (make C {v:1}) c set "w" 9
column3: class instances are sealed — an undeclared field cannot be set
a declared return is enforced — String can never be Integer
…in either direction
strict list index misses loudly

column1: do [{a:1} !. b] error [dot message] eq 'getr: key "b" not found in map'
column3: the strict-miss message is readable off the caught Error

column1: # §4  `error` is a pattern match — a no-op on every non-Error top

column3: an Integer passes through; the handler never runs
a String passes through
None is not an Error
a List passes through
a Map passes through
only the TOP of stack is matched; deeper values are untouched
chained error words are all no-ops on a success value

column1: # §5  boru:test assertions — pass, fail, and sequencing

column3: a passing Assert.equal returns nothing and execution continues
a passing Assert.not-equal is silent
any truthy value passes Assert.ok
a contained substring passes Assert.match
a raising body passes Assert.throws
equal sides fail not-equal
none is falsy for Assert.ok
a missing substring fails Assert.match
a non-raising body fails Assert.throws
Test.test catches an assertion_failure and records it — later cases still run
…a falsy Assert.ok records the same way
